title: Robustness of Speech Denoising Models
one_liner: Deep speech denoising models fail catastrophically when adversarial noise is hidden inside real audio, undetectable to human ears.
lead: Speech denoising models remove background noise from audio before it reaches humans or transcription systems. They are used everywhere: hearing aids, video calls, voice assistants, emergency dispatch. This paper proves that despite working perfectly on normal noisy audio, four recent denoising models can be broken by adding a second type of noise that sounds completely silent to people but destroys the model's output.

problem.h2: Speech denoising broke by silent noise
paras: Speech denoising is simple in concept: a model listens to messy audio (voice plus jackhammer, traffic, office chatter) and outputs just the voice. These models work well on real noise because they were trained on real examples. They are deployed in phones, hearing aids, emergency 911 systems, and voice assistants because they solve a real problem.

A beginner might assume once a model handles background noise correctly, nothing else can break it. The trap: the model learned patterns from one type of noise (random hiss, traffic rumble, speech babble). A different type of noise — one designed specifically to fool this exact model — might slip past entirely, unnoticed by any human listening, yet reduce the output to complete gibberish.

callout.html: Add invisible adversarial noise to speech audio, and the denoising model produces garbage, while humans still hear only the original clean speech.

paras: The paper reveals a flaw in how denoising models process audio. The model itself does not change. What changes is the understanding: the hidden assumption that surviving normal noise means surviving all perturbations is false.

hidden.h2: Imperceptibility to humans versus model failure
hidden.name: Psychoacoustic concealment
paras: Psychoacoustics is the study of what humans actually hear. Not all sound frequencies matter equally to human ears. Some frequencies are easier for humans to detect than others. Some sounds mask other sounds. Psychoacoustic concealment means hiding one sound inside another sound in a way that takes advantage of these human hearing limits.

This paper measures whether adversarial noise stays hidden from human perception while simultaneously breaking the model's output. It tests this with human expert listeners using ABX listening tests (side-by-side audio comparison where judges say whether two samples are the same or different). When the adversarial noise is psychoacoustically hidden, humans report the audio sounds identical, but transcription accuracy on the model output drops to near zero.

heat.caption: Darker means adversarial noise concentrates here; these frequencies hide from human ears but break the model.

reads.html: The attack hides tiny noise in audio ranges humans ignore, like the sizzle of speaker static or the hum behind your vision at a concert.
The adversarial perturbation exploits psychoacoustic masking and threshold effects to minimize human perceptibility while maximizing model error rate.

mechanism.h2: Why adversarial noise breaks denoising models
paras: A denoising model learns a specific pattern: what does speech look like when mixed with real noise (traffic, wind, hum). It memorizes how to separate them. The model is blind to other patterns that look equally valid mathematically but do not look like natural noise.

Adversarial noise is noise that is mathematically optimized to fool this specific model, not designed to sound like real-world noise. The model has no learned defense against it because it never trained on examples of this kind of perturbation. Meanwhile, humans do not perceive adversarial noise because the noise is constructed at frequencies and intensities just below human hearing thresholds — a completely different problem than denoising real background noise. The model and humans solve two different sensing problems, and adversarial noise exposes the gap.

In high-stakes applications like 911 dispatch or medical transcription, the model's output is trusted because it works on normal cases. This paper shows that trust is misplaced: the model can silently fail on adversarial input, producing garbage while appearing to work perfectly.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start with audio signal strength 1.0 (normal speech + background noise).
Optimize adversarial perturbation delta to maximize model error.
Check: delta has loudness 0.05, below human hearing threshold of 0.07, so imperceptible.
Final audio is 1.0 (original) plus 0.05 (adversarial), undetectable to humans.
Model receives input 1.05, but training data never showed this pattern, so output becomes corrupted gibberish.
Perceptibility constraint lambda multiplier kept the noise small enough that humans report audio unchanged (ABX test same), proving imperceptibility.
Meanwhile transcription of model output drops from 95 percent correct to 2 percent — model has failed silently.

math.note: The gradient-based optimizer finds noise that minimizes what the model is confident about, subject to the noise remaining invisible to human hearing.

items.html: Adversarial noise optimized for one denoising model does not reliably break other models. Each model has a different blind spot.
Adversarial noise might lose its power if played through speakers and re-recorded (air gap)? The paper shows this is not a complete defense — some attacks survive this channel.
Designing adversarial noise that produces a specific target output (not just gibberish) is much harder than untargeted attacks that just maximize error.
Real countermeasures would need to mix adversarial training (training on adversarial examples), input filtering, and loss functions designed to defend against both natural and adversarial noise.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple speech denoising model trained only on real background noise (traffic, office chatter, wind). Then attack it with gradient-based adversarial noise at imperceptibility levels (loudness just below human hearing threshold). Test three things: (1) Run ABX listening tests with humans to confirm noise is imperceptible. (2) Feed the attacked audio to the trained model and measure transcription error rate. (3) Try the same adversarial noise on a different denoising model and check if it transfers.
demo.metric_eq: attack_success = (transcription_error_after_attack > 80 percent) AND (human_imperceptibility_test > 70 percent agree sounds identical)
demo.closing: The demo proves the core vulnerability: a model can fail silently on imperceptible perturbations while appearing confident, a risk in any safety-critical application.
